units.title: OP Stack chains with a non-ETH gas token
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 14 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Leads L-692, L-726 and L-725. Monad validators may execute hot contracts as native code from Monad's own x86 compiler (category-labs/monad, tag v0.16.7 and the mainnet-listed v0.16.5; compiler under category/vm/compiler, emitter in ir/x86), while every RPC node interprets. Cycle 14 showed that mined results are certified by the validators, so compiled code has agreed with the interpreter on every input that was mined. These PoolManager paths have never been mined on Monad: clear of an exact credit (src/PoolManager.sol clear), transferFrom and burn through an allowance or an operator (src/ERC6909.sol, src/ERC6909Claims.sol), approve, donate (src/libraries/Pool.sol donate), the overflow fallback of getNextSqrtPriceFromAmount0RoundingUp (src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol), and amounts above 2^160. Task 1: for each of those paths, take the exact basic blocks of the built bytecode (use jumpmap.json and a disassembly of build/PoolManager.json) and list their instruction sequences. For each instruction say which emitter routine Monad uses given what the compiler knows at that point: constant operands (shifts, masks, MULMOD or DIV by a constant, comparisons against constants), operands in registers, AVX registers or stack slots, comparison results kept in CPU flags until JUMPI, the same value used twice, and stack depth at block entry and exit. Model each distinct routine in Python from the C++ source, instruction by instruction, and run the block's inputs through the model and through pyevm.py on at least 100,000 random and edge inputs per routine. Plant a fault to show the comparison can fail. Report every routine with file and line and whether it matches. Task 2 (L-726): decide whether the PoolManager is compiled at all. The compiler gives up when its size estimate passes 10,240 + 32 times the code size (778,528 bytes for 24,009 bytes; compiler/ir/x86.hpp and x86.cpp). Either build the emitter with stubbed runtime symbols from downloaded source (asmjit is vendored or named in CMakeLists.txt) and print the estimate for the PoolManager runtime, or bound the estimate from below and above by summing the emitted bytes per instruction from the source. Say which it is. Task 3 (L-725): which execution mode do validators run by default (Dual or InterpreterOnly), from the node's command line defaults and the published validator instructions, and after how much gas of interpretation is a contract compiled? A routine that departs from the EVM specification on an input the PoolManager can produce is a finding an ordinary account could use; give the input.

Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Leads L-720 and L-744. reth v2.11.0 (Ethereum) ships an LLVM based compiler for EVM code, evm2-jit, which builds and validates blocks when a node operator turns it on with --jit or the reth_jit RPC (F-129). Tempo v1.19.1 pins a later revision and leaves it out of release builds. No simulated call uses it, so its opcode results have never been tested by this review. Source: https://github.com/DaniPopes/evm2 (also reachable as alloy-rs/evm2), crates/jit, at revisions 66687c18b34d3bdbb899f5eb7605070615c03475 (reth v2.11.0) and 35aa32800b147b00e616d4e1869a3835aa86701f (Tempo v1.19.1). Read the code generation for every opcode the PoolManager runtime contains (disassemble build/PoolManager.json for the list), with most care for: MULMOD with modulus 2^256-1 and with the constant moduli 2^96 and 2^128, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV and SMOD at -2^255 and -1, MOD, EXP, SIGNEXTEND from every byte index including 31 and above, BYTE with index above 31, SHL, SHR and SAR with counts of 255, 256 and above 2^64, the comparisons, ISZERO chains fused with JUMPI, dynamic JUMP through the jump table, the bytecode analysis passes that merge or drop blocks (crates/jit/codegen/src/bytecode/passes, including block_analysis.rs, which changed between the two revisions), constant folding and peephole rules, stack depth checks at block entry, gas accounting per block against the interpreter's per instruction accounting on an out-of-gas halt, memory expansion with MCOPY and KECCAK256, CALLDATALOAD and CALLDATACOPY past the end, RETURNDATACOPY bounds, TLOAD and TSTORE with the static call check, and the builtins the compiled code calls for the rest (crates/jit/builtins). For each folding or lowering rule that is not a plain call into the interpreter's own routine, transcribe it in Python and run it against pyevm.py on the vectors of research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/targeted.py and battery.py plus edge cases of your own, and plant a fault to show the comparison can fail. If the crate builds here with the LLVM that rustc ships or without LLVM for its tests, say so and run its own differential tests on the PoolManager runtime; otherwise work from the source. Also say how a node decides to compile a contract (hot threshold, maximum bytecode length against 24,009 bytes), whether compiled and interpreted execution can be mixed inside one transaction, and what happens to a block when the two disagree on Ethereum, where other clients exist, and on Tempo, where they do not. A rule that departs from the specification on an input the PoolManager can produce is a finding; give the input and the source line.

Leads L-738, L-728, L-626, L-732, L-618 and L-748. HyperEVM's validator (hl-node) and MegaETH's sequencer executor are closed, so evidence about them comes from mined data. Cycle 14's work is in research/network-risk/cycles/014/theme-producer-operands.work and cycle 13's in research/network-risk/cycles/013/theme-mined-branches.work and theme-swap-residuals.work (replay2.py). (1) L-738, HyperEVM: find the highest volume Uniswap v3 style pools (PoolCreated logs of their factories from the archive client at https://rpc.purroofgroup.com). For every mined swap in the last 2,000,000 blocks whose step needs a product at or above 2^256, an amount at or above 2^160, the overflow fallback of getNextSqrtPriceFromAmount0RoundingUp, or that ends on an initialized tick, check the logged amounts, price and tick against the exact FullMath, SqrtPriceMath and TickMath formulas from parent-block state. Report counts per branch and plant a fault to show the check can fail. (2) L-728: scan the full history of PoolManager transactions on MegaETH and HyperEVM for calls to clear() and say whether any clears an exact credit, and replay those in the reference interpreter against the receipts and storage. (3) L-626 and L-732, MegaETH: build the public stateless validator from the mega-evm repository with cargo in your work directory (crates come from crates.io and GitHub, which are reachable) and run it on recent blocks that contain PoolManager transactions, using the witness method the public RPC offers. If it cannot be built or fed, say exactly which step fails. From the public mega-reth or mega-evm lock, name the reth revision and say whether its execution cache has the branch that keeps cached storage of a destroyed and re-created account without code (reth cached_state.rs, fixed by reth pull request 28148). (4) L-618 and L-748, HyperEVM: anything public that names the EVM library versions inside hl-node, and the HyperCore action that produced the first unsigned system transfer in the name of 0xc20699185c15D0a2fD65779BB5d69f5b0B113c00. Record any mismatch between mined data and the exact formulas as a finding with the transaction hash.

A reading of v4-core itself at the places where a network difference could change its logic, with the bytecode next to the source. research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json lists 387 conditional jumps; 338 were taken both ways by the six script sets and 49 are recorded as unreachable guards or repeated tests. Task 1: recheck the 49. For each, give the source line, the two sides, and the exact condition under which the untaken side would run. Then say whether any of the 21 networks could make that condition true where Ethereum cannot: a different result of CALL, STATICCALL, RETURNDATASIZE, EXTCODESIZE, BALANCE, SELFBALANCE, CALLVALUE, GAS, TLOAD after a revert, or of a precompile or system contract named as currency, hook or recipient (see state/networks.json and ASSUMPTIONS.md for the per network lists). Where a side is reachable on some network, build a script with state overrides in the style of research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pmdiff6.py, run it on that network and on the reference interpreter, and report the result. Task 2: list every place where the source depends on a property of the EVM that is not an opcode result: transient storage cleared at the end of the transaction (src/libraries/Lock.sol, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol, CurrencyDelta.sol, CurrencyReserves.sol), msg.value seen once per call frame (src/PoolManager.sol settle and settleFor), reverts rolling back transient writes, the 63/64 gas rule around hook calls and token calls (src/libraries/Hooks.sol, src/types/Currency.sol), returndata of a call to an address without code, the order of events, and the dirty upper bits that assembly blocks clean or assume clean (every and(), shl() and signextend() in assembly in src/). For each, name the networks whose transaction types or execution contexts could break it (batched and sponsored transactions on Tempo, system transactions on HyperEVM, retryables and Stylus on Arbitrum, deposits on the OP Stack, mini-blocks on MegaETH, parallel execution with re-execution on Monad, Polygon and BNB Chain, account abstraction bundles everywhere) and test it with a simulated call or a mined transaction where possible. Task 3: for the assembly blocks in src/ that read or write memory without the free memory pointer discipline (CustomRevert, Hooks.callHook, Currency transfer, the extsload paths in src/Extsload.sol and src/Exttload.sol, ParseBytes, Position.calculatePositionKey), say what each assumes about memory above the free pointer and about returndata size, and check the assumption in the built bytecode by running the edge inputs in pyevm.py and on three networks with different clients. Report anything where a network can make the PoolManager take a side or read a value that Ethereum cannot produce, with the input, as a finding.
